question: A 63-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of progressive blurring and darkening of her vision in the right eye. Upon waking up in the morning, she suddenly started seeing multiple dark streaks. She has migraines and type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed at her last health maintenance examination 20 years ago. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Her only medication is sumatriptan. Her vitals are within normal limits. Ophthalmologic examination shows visual acuity of 20/40 in the left eye and 20/100 in the right eye. The fundus is obscured and difficult to visualize on fundoscopic examination of the right eye. The red reflex is diminished on the right. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Progressive blurring and darkening of vision" -> "Sudden onset" -> "Multiple dark streaks" -> "Fundus obscured" -> "Diminished red reflex" -> "Vitreous hemorrhage" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Progressive blurring and darkening of vision" -> "Sudden onset" -> "Multiple dark streaks" -> "Fundus obscured" -> "Diminished red reflex" -> "Central retinal vein occlusion" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Progressive blurring and darkening of vision" -> "Sudden onset" -> "Multiple dark streaks" -> "Fundus obscured" -> "Diminished red reflex" -> "Cataract" -> 50%
CHAIN: "Progressive blurring and darkening of vision" -> "Sudden onset" -> "Multiple dark streaks" -> "Fundus obscured" -> "Diminished red reflex" -> "Central retinal artery occlusion" -> 40%
CHAIN: "Progressive blurring and darkening of vision" -> "Sudden onset" -> "Multiple dark streaks" -> "Fundus obscured" -> "Diminished red reflex" -> "Migraine aura" -> 30%
analysis: The patient's symptoms and examination findings are suggestive of a vitreous hemorrhage. The sudden onset of vision changes, including blurring and dark streaks, along with a diminished red reflex and obscured fundus, align with this diagnosis. The patient's history of diabetes increases the risk for retinal complications, such as vitreous hemorrhage due to proliferative diabetic retinopathy. Other options like central retinal vein or artery occlusion would typically present with different fundoscopic findings, such as retinal hemorrhages or a cherry-red spot, respectively. A cataract would not cause sudden vision changes, and a migraine aura would not cause a diminished red reflex or obscured fundus.
